explanations.explanation: Gad it is. The LORD asks, “Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad?” Gad was one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 35:26), and the LORD's first question is “Has Israel no sons?” That's a lot like finding a stranger sitting in a chair with your name on it, and the LORD wants to know why.

Reuben was one of Jacob's sons, Jacob's firstborn in fact (Genesis 35:23), so I get the guess. But the verse names Gad. The LORD asks, “Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad?” Easy to mix up when Jacob had so many sons.

Close, friend! Asher stands right beside Gad in the list of Jacob's sons (Genesis 35:26). But the LORD names Gad. He asks, “Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad?” Gad is the one in the question.

A heap of ruins. The LORD says Rabbah “…will become a heap of ruins, and its villages will be burned.” I think this is one of the heavy parts, friend. It's the LORD speaking about a real city and a real judgment, and the passage doesn't soften it.

A city of refuge is a place of safety, where people could run for protection (Numbers 35:11). The LORD says nothing like that here. He says Rabbah will become a heap of ruins, and its villages will be burned. That's about as far from a safe place as it gets.

A fortress is built up, and this verse is about what gets torn down. The LORD says Rabbah “…will become a heap of ruins…” Its villages will be burned too. A strong city is a natural thing to picture, friend, but that's not what the verse says.

True. After Rabbah falls, the LORD says, “Then Israel will drive out their dispossessors, says the LORD.” The ones who pushed Israel out will be the ones pushed out. It's a turnaround, and this verse puts it in the LORD's own words.

The text says otherwise, friend. The LORD says, “Then Israel will drive out their dispossessors, says the LORD.” Dispossessors are the people who took the land. So Israel is the one doing the driving out in this verse.

His priests and officials. The LORD says, “…Milcom will go into exile together with his priests and officials.” So the god and the ones named with him go into exile together. The verse names priests and officials, and no one else.

Horses and chariots are a fair guess for a king's company, friend, but the verse doesn't mention them. It says Milcom will go into exile “…together with his priests and officials.” Those are the ones who go along.
Musicians and singers aren't listed, friend. The text says Milcom will go into exile “…together with his priests and officials.” Those are the ones named.

Riches. The LORD says, “You trust in your riches and say, ‘Who can come against me?’” That's a big question to ask when your trust is in your money. I've been guilty of trusting my own stamp work too much, and it never ends well.

Prophets are never mentioned in this charge. The LORD says, “You trust in your riches and say, ‘Who can come against me?’” The valleys are fruitful, and she boasts about them. So the trust is in what she owns.

Allies aren't named here, friend. The LORD says, “You trust in your riches and say, ‘Who can come against me?’” Then the terror comes “…from all those around you.” The trust is in riches, and nothing in the verse says who stood beside her.

Not quite. The LORD says the Ammonites will be “…driven headlong, with no one to regather the fugitives.” So nobody is going to gather them back up. That's a lonely picture, and I think it's meant to sting.
False. The verse says, “You will each be driven headlong, with no one to regather the fugitives.” Nobody is waiting to round them up. That makes the promise coming in verse 6 stand out all the more.
Restore them. The LORD says, “Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity…” All that heavy talk, and then one little word turns it. Friend, that “Yet” is doing some serious lifting.

explanations.answer: Give the Ammonites' land to Moab
explanations.explanation: Moab doesn't show up in these verses at all. The LORD says, “Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity…” The promise is about the Ammonites themselves being restored. Nothing here hands their land to someone else.

The LORD does say Rabbah will become a heap of ruins (Jeremiah 49:2), but nothing in the passage says it stays empty for good. The LORD says, “Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity…” One word, “Yet,” turns the whole message. The last thing He says about the Ammonites is restoration.

explanations.answer: Turn and run and lie low
explanations.explanation: Turn and run and lie low. The LORD says, “Turn and run! Lie low, O dwellers of Dedan, for I will bring disaster on Esau at the time I punish him.” That's a plain warning. If someone told me to run, I'd leave the dough right where it sat.
Nobody is told to fight. The LORD says to the dwellers of Dedan, “Turn and run! Lie low…” The disaster is coming on Esau at the time He punishes him. The instruction is to get out of the way.
No soldiers are sent anywhere in this verse. The LORD says, “Turn and run! Lie low, O dwellers of Dedan…” Teman was named in verse 7, but Dedan isn't told to march there. It's told to hide.

Strip him bare. The LORD asks about grape gatherers and thieves, and then says, “But I will strip Esau bare…” Grape gatherers leave some gleanings and thieves take only what they want. This is far beyond either one. The “But” marks the turn.
That's what the question in verse 9 pictures, friend. Grape gatherers would leave some gleanings. But then the LORD says, “But I will strip Esau bare…” The “But” tells you the answer is the opposite.
Taking only what you want sounds like the thieves in verse 9. Then the LORD turns it around: “But I will strip Esau bare…” Gold isn't mentioned. The picture is of nothing left to hold on to.
The LORD says the opposite. He says, “I will uncover his hiding places, and he will be unable to conceal himself.” So the hiding places get found. Esau won't have a spot to tuck himself away.
False. The LORD says, “I will uncover his hiding places, and he will be unable to conceal himself.” His hiding places get uncovered. He can't hide, and that's the whole point of the verse.

Preserve. The LORD says, “Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives.” Right in the middle of a heavy passage, there's a promise to keep orphans alive. I think that's a tender thing to find here, friend.
Test isn't the word. The LORD says, “Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives.” It's a promise to keep them alive. Nothing in the verse says He is putting them through anything.

Judgment fills the passage around this verse, so I see why you picked it. But here the LORD says, “Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives.” For the orphans, the word is preserve. It's a small bright spot in a heavy stretch.

True. The LORD asks, “If those who do not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, can you possibly remain unpunished?” Then He says, “You will not go unpunished, for you must drink it too.” The verse says Edom drinks the cup too.
The verse says the opposite, friend. The LORD says, “You will not go unpunished, for you must drink it too.” Edom doesn't get to skip the cup. It drinks it too.

By Himself. The LORD says, “For by Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD…” That's the highest kind of oath there is. Scripture says that when God made His promise to Abraham, He had no one greater to swear by, so He swore by Himself (Hebrews 6:13).
The heavens aren't named in this oath. The LORD says, “For by Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD…” He swears by Himself. No one else is named.
The temple doesn't come up in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “For by Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD…” He swears by Himself. That makes the oath about as solid as an oath can be.
That's not what the verse says. The LORD says Bozrah's cities “…will be in ruins forever.” Forever is the opposite of a short while. There's no rebuilding in this verse.
False. The LORD says, “…all her cities will be in ruins forever.” Forever doesn't leave room for a short while. I think this one is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: Assemble and rise up for battle
explanations.explanation: Assemble and rise up. The envoy's message is, “Assemble yourselves to march against her! Rise up for battle!” The nations are being called to gather and march against Edom. It's a call to arms, not a call to a party.

explanations.answer: Gather and bring gifts of peace
explanations.explanation: Gathering is right, but the gifts aren't in the text. The message says, “Assemble yourselves to march against her! Rise up for battle!” It's a call to march, friend. Nobody is told to bring a thing.
Staying home isn't what the envoy says. The message is, “Assemble yourselves to march against her! Rise up for battle!” The nations are told to get up and go. Watching from the porch isn't an option.

Pride. The LORD says, “The terror you cause and the pride of your heart have deceived you…” Pride can fool a person right out of their senses. I've been fooled by my own pride more than once, mostly about how straight I was pressing.

Fear sounds close to the terror Edom causes, but it isn't the word in the blank. The LORD says, “The terror you cause and the pride of your heart have deceived you…” The word that fits is pride. The verse names both the terror and the pride.
Grief isn't what the LORD points to here, friend. He says, “The terror you cause and the pride of your heart have deceived you…” The word is pride. It's the heart of the proud that gets fooled.

He brings Edom down. The LORD says, “Though you elevate your nest like the eagle, even from there I will bring you down…” declares the LORD. A nest up high feels safe, but height doesn't stop Him. Edom's high place doesn't change the outcome.

Higher is the opposite direction, friend. The LORD says, “Though you elevate your nest like the eagle, even from there I will bring you down…” The nest is already high, and He brings Edom down from it.

A high nest does sound safe, but that's not what the LORD says. He says, “Though you elevate your nest like the eagle, even from there I will bring you down…” The height doesn't protect Edom. He brings them down.

True. The LORD says, “Edom will become an object of horror. All who pass by will be appalled and will scoff at all her wounds.” I think this part is heavy, friend. Those passing by are appalled, and they scoff.
The verse says otherwise. The LORD says, “All who pass by will be appalled and will scoff at all her wounds.” So the passersby do scoff. It's a heavy picture, and the text says it plainly.

Sodom and Gomorrah, two cities that were overthrown (Genesis 19:24-25). The LORD says, “As Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown along with their neighbors… no one will dwell there; no man will abide there.” That's the comparison He picks for Edom's future. It's a heavy one.

Tyre and Sidon are real cities, but the LORD doesn't name them here. He says, “As Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown along with their neighbors…” Those are the two cities in the comparison. They were overthrown, and so will Edom be emptied.

Jericho and Bethel are real places too, friend, but they aren't in this verse. The LORD says, “As Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown along with their neighbors…” Those two cities were overthrown (Genesis 19:24-25). That's the picture for Edom.

That's the opposite of what the LORD says. He asks, “For who is like Me, and who can challenge Me? What shepherd can stand against Me?” The question is meant to be answered with no one. There's no shepherd who can stand against Him.
False. The LORD asks, “For who is like Me, and who can challenge Me? What shepherd can stand against Me?” The questions answer themselves. No one is like Him, and no shepherd can stand against Him.

The text says the opposite. It speaks of the plans the LORD has drawn up against Edom, and then says, “Surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away…” Their pasture will be made desolate too. I think this is a sad line, and it's not safe for the little ones.

False. The verse speaks of the plans the LORD has drawn up against Edom, and then says, “Surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away; certainly their pasture will be made desolate because of them.” They aren't kept safe. It's a heavy line, friend, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Quake. The passage says, “At the sound of their fall the earth will quake; their cry will resound to the Red Sea.” The earth shakes at the sound of the fall. The cry carries all the way to the Red Sea.
Rejoicing isn't in this verse, friend. The passage says, “At the sound of their fall the earth will quake…” The earth shakes. The cry carries all the way to the Red Sea.
Rest is the opposite of what the verse says. The passage says, “At the sound of their fall the earth will quake…” The sound of Edom's fall shakes the earth. Nothing about it is restful.

explanations.answer: The heart of a woman in labor
explanations.explanation: That's the picture. The passage says, “In that day the hearts of Edom’s mighty men will be like the heart of a woman in labor.” These are the mighty men, and their hearts are anything but mighty. Notice the word “like.” It's a comparison, and the text doesn't say more than that.

explanations.answer: The heart of a roaring lion
explanations.explanation: A lion does appear earlier, in verse 19, as a picture of one who comes up against Edom. It's not a picture of Edom's own men. The passage says their hearts will be “…like the heart of a woman in labor.” These mighty men aren't roaring.

explanations.answer: The heart of a proud king
explanations.explanation: Pride does show up in this passage, in verse 16. But the passage doesn't say Edom's mighty men have a king's heart. It says, “In that day the hearts of Edom’s mighty men will be like the heart of a woman in labor.”
